title: Cardinals sign ex-Lions third round pick
description: The Arizona Cardinals made a defensive line addition by signing former Lions third-round pick Brodric Martin.
fullText:
Cardinals sign ex-Lions third round pick appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The Arizona Cardinals on Saturday signed defensive tackle Brodric Martin after bringing him in for a workout with three other interior defensive linemen on Friday. Martin was one of four players evaluated by Arizona, alongside Evan Anderson, Casey Rogers, and Keveion’ta Spears.

The signing could be connected to the apparent left knee injury suffered by defensive tackle Walter Nolen during practice on Saturday. The transaction may simply provide additional depth on the defensive line while the Cardinals assess Nolen’s condition.

After playing college football at North Alabama and Western Kentucky, Martin was selected by the Detroit Lions with the No. 96 overall pick in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft. He appeared in three games during his rookie season with Detroit in 2023 before opening the 2024 campaign on injured reserve. Martin was activated on Nov. 20 that season.

Uros Medic (13-3) is the No. 14 fighter in the UFC’s welterweight division rankings. The 33-year-old Serbian has not fought in his home country during his professional career, which began in Alaska in 2016.

title: New York Yankees Predicted to Land 3-Time All-Star Before Trade Deadline
description: The New York Yankees are expected to be one of the most aggressive teams in the days leading up to Monday’s MLB trade deadline.Reports have connected the Yankees to several players as the front office looks to add bullpen help, a right-handed bat, and a catcher while the team continues to battle injuries across its […] The post New York Yankees Predicted to Land 3-Time All-Star Before Trade Deadline appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The New York Yankees are expected to be one of the most aggressive teams in the days leading up to Monday’s MLB trade deadline.

Reports have connected the Yankees to several players as the front office looks to add bullpen help, a right-handed bat, and a catcher while the team continues to battle injuries across its roster.

On Friday night, ESPN’s Jeff Passan appeared on SportsCenter and shared several of his trade deadline predictions, including one involving the Yankees.

While acknowledging that many Yankees fans want the team to land San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller, Passan predicted New York will make a rare in-division trade for three-time All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles.

Rutschman is currently on the 10-day injured list with left wrist inflammation, but he is expected to resume hitting Saturday. That timeline likely won’t stop the Yankees from pursuing him, especially with catcher remaining one of their biggest needs.

“I know Yankees fans want Mason Miller, but they also want a catcher, and we’re gonna give them an in-division trade in Adley Rutschman,” Passan said. “Now, Adley Rutschman’s on the injured list right now. But the Orioles, who are looking at dealing Rutschman, potentially Jackson Holliday potentially as well, they’re trying to get back to 2023 when they won 101 games, and Adley Rutschman, switch hitter, a leader, is absolutely perfect for the Yankees.”

MLB trade matchmaker ⚾️@JeffPassan picks the best trade candidates for the Yankees, Cubs, Dodgers and Brewers 👀 pic.twitter.com/UIUO7cjhmP

— SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) July 31, 2026

Rutschman earned his third All-Star selection this season despite appearing in just 67 games.

He’s batting .251 with 30 runs, 62 hits, eight home runs, and 47 RBIs, while posting a .433 slugging percentage and a .764 OPS.

The Yankees have primarily split catching duties between Austin Wells and Ali Sánchez this season. Adding Rutschman would immediately give them an everyday-caliber starter who is still just 28 years old and under club control through the 2027 season.

title: “Gave my life, heart and soul”: Howe resigns from Newcastle, hails fans and “privilege of my lifetime”
description: Eddie Howe has called the opportunity to manage Newcastle United the 'privilege of my lifetime' after stepping down from his role as head coach.Howe has made the decision to leave Newcastle after five...
fullText:
Eddie Howe has called the opportunity to manage Newcastle United the 'privilege of my lifetime' after stepping down from his role as head coach.

Howe has made the decision to leave Newcastle after five years in charge, after informing the board of his desire to take a break from football.

The 48-year-old leaves Newcastle having ended the club's 70-year wait for a major trophy by lifting the League Cup in 2025.

He also twice guided the Magpies toChampions League qualification, ending a 20-year absence from Europe's top competition, having inherited a side struggling at the bottom of the table in November 2021.

Howe has now decided that now is the time to step down at St James' Park, with German coach Matthias Jaissle set to replace him. Newcastle have agreed a compensation package with Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli for the 38-year-old.

In a statement confirming his exit, Howe said his time in the North East has been the highlight of his coaching career.

“After a period of personal reflection, I have decided that now is the right time for me to step away from my role as head coach of Newcastle United.

“After nearly five years of giving my life, heart and soul into the club with unrelenting energy, I feel that it is in the best interests of both myself and the club to step away, recharge and take a break.

“Although it’s been incredibly difficult to make this decision, I know in my heart that it’s the right one. I have always put the best interests of Newcastle before my own in every single decision I have made whilst I’ve been here and this one is no different.

“It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have been the manager of Newcastle United.

“It is difficult to put into words what this club, the city and its supporters mean, and will always mean, to me and my family. From the moment myself, Jason and all of the staff arrived nearly half a decade ago, Newcastle instantly felt like home and the people here welcomed us with open arms. We took huge pride in representing the club from day one and this city will always hold a very special place in our hearts.

“There have been so many incredible moments in our time here. From fighting relegation in our first season to the numerous unforgettable nights at St. James’ Park in the Champions League soon after. The progression was fast.

“Everyone came together, united and what a force we became, culminating in bringing home our first domestic trophy in 70 years. These are all memories that I will cherish for the rest of my life.

“I would like to put on record my sincere thanks and appreciation to Yasir Al-Rumayyan, Jamie Reuben, Jacobo Solís and everyone at PIF, David Hopkinson, Ross Wilson and the entire ownership and leadership group for placing their trust in me and for giving me the opportunity to lead this special football club.

“I remain incredibly positive and enthusiastic about the future of Newcastle. The club is in fantastic hands with a great leadership team and I have no doubt together, alongside whoever comes in to replace me, they will continue to deliver success on the pitch.

“Thank you to Jason Tindall, Graeme Jones, Stephen Purches, Simon Weatherstone, Dan Hodges, Andy Howe and Jordan Tribe for their incredible loyalty, support and dedication and to all of the amazing staff behind the scenes whose hard work and loyalty makes this club what it is.

“A special thank you to all of the players who have represented the club during my time here. Without you, nothing would have been possible and it’s been an honour to have coached you all.

“Finally, and most importantly, thank you to our incredible supporters. Your passion and loyalty have inspired me every single day. To stand on the touchline at St. James’ Park as your manager with the honour of representing your club has meant more to me than you will ever know.

“While my journey as manager has now come to an end, the affinity and love I will always hold for Newcastle United never will.

“Thank you for everything. I wish the club every success for the future.”

fullText:
Usman Nurmagomedov knocked out Archie Colgan in the first round to retain the PFL Lightweight World Championship in the PFL New York main event on Friday.

UBS Arena played host to an night of mixed martial arts as PFL New York lit up the Big Apple with unforgettable performances and thrilling finishes. The event comes on the heels of yesterday’s landmark merger announcement between MVP and the PFL. MVP Co-Founders, Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidaria, joined Chief Executive Officer John Martin cageside for the event which created the new platform under the MVP banner. Several global combat sports stars were in attendance to witness this incredible night of action including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Islam Machachev, Kamaru Usman, Royce Gracie and PFL Interim World Champion Johnny Eblen. 

Nurmagomedov (22-0, 1NC) continued his reign of dominance with a first round TKO of previously-undefeated challenger No. 3 Archie “King” Colgan (13-1) to retain the PFL Lightweight World Championship. Nurmagomedov put his striking arsenal on full display as he dropped Colgan with a well-placed head kick followed by a left hook. Colgan survived momentarily, but the champ put the challenger away with a pair of brutal uppercuts and ground and pound, all in the opening round. 

The co-main event saw the triumphant return of No. 1 “Dangerous” Dakota Ditcheva(16-0), as she defeated No. 6 Denise “Miss Dynamite” Kielholtz (9-6) by unanimous decision. Stepping into the cage for the first time in over a year, Ditcheva looked as sharp as ever, as she put on a striking clinic and landed a takedown. Kielholtz gave a valiant effort, but in the end, the PFL’s top Women’s Flyweight was just too much to handle. 

In a dominant display of striking skills, No. 10 Amru Magomedov(11-0) took Angel “Salsa King” Alvarez(11-3) en route to a second-round TKO win. From the opening bell, Magomedov used his kicks to devastating effect, punishing Alvarez’s legs. Magomedov chopped Alvarez down with a leg kick in the second round, and finished things off with an avalanche of ground and pound from full mount. 

Moustapha Diakhate (6-0-1) kicked off the main card with a bang, as he crushed Darryl “The Sacred Beast” Walker(2-1) by TKO in the opening round. Diakhate, who was fighting for the first time on American soil, scored an early takedown and eventually got to full mount. From there, it was all Diakhate, as he punished Walker with heavy strikes to get the stoppage win and make a massive statement in his PFL debut.

title: Hardik Pandya stayed at his home before IPL stardom: Australia hopeful Jerrssis Wadia opens up on his Mumbai, Bollywood roots
description: Australian cricket star Jerrssis Wadia opens up about his Bollywood family roots and reveals how Hardik Pandya stayed at his home before making it big in the IPL.
fullText:
Hardik Pandya stayed at his home before IPL stardom: Australia hopeful Jerrssis Wadia opens up on his Mumbai, Bollywood roots originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Australia's Jerrssis Wadia reveals Hardik Pandya once lived with his family.

Wadia's Bollywood-actor father and Guinness record-holding grandfather shaped his cricket journey.

Australia hopeful eyes Big Bash title, Shield cricket, and national selection.

An Indian-origin cricketer chasing an Australian cap has revealed an unlikely connection to Indian cricket royalty, with Jerrssis Wadia disclosing that Hardik Pandya once stayed at his family's Mumbai home in the years before he became a household name in the IPL.

The 24-year-old Wadia made waves last season for Adelaide Strikers by smashing his first three deliveries for six against Brisbane Heat in only his second Big Bash appearance. That moment instantly turned him from a relatively unknown quantity into a name Australian cricket fans started paying attention to.

His father Dillzan works as an actor in Bollywood, while his grandfather Neville holds a Guinness World Record as the oldest person to score a century in minor cricket. It was his grandfather, in fact, who first sparked his passion for the sport during his childhood.

MORE: Hardik Pandya trade: MI want CSK duo as part of swap deal, Chennai Super Kings ready to offer cash-plus one player to sign Mumbai Indians captain

And growing up around his grandparents also brought Wadia into contact with a young Hardik and Krunal Pandya, and that early relationship blossomed into a lasting bond. Wadia explained that his family had supported the Pandya brothers with their education when they were still children, which laid the foundation for a friendship that grew stronger over the years.

"My family helped out Hardik and Krunal with their education when they were kids, and our relationship kind of went from there," he told Cricket AU. "My dad, Hardik and Krunal all played cricket together and the bond got really strong."

He recalled that when Hardik first broke into the IPL with Mumbai Indians and had nowhere to stay in the city, he ended up living with Wadia's parents for a while. That connection has stayed alive over the years, with Wadia receiving messages of encouragement from both brothers after being picked for the Cricket Australia XI and again following his Big Bash debut.

"When Hardik came onto the scene in the IPL, he stayed with my parents for a bit because he played for Mumbai Indians and he didn't have a place in Mumbai," he said.

"I got a text from Hardik and Krunal after (I was selected in) the CA XI, as well as after my Big Bash debut. It's amazing to have support like that and to have someone who's already dominated at the top level but is still humble enough to talk and guide me whenever he can.

"Not everyone would have the privilege to talk to players who are at that level, especially Indian cricketers. They're like rock stars."

MORE: MI captain for IPL 2027: Bumrah and Tilak emerge as contenders

Wadia's story is a nice example of how personal relationships in cricket can quietly shape careers years down the line, long before fame enters the picture. Few would have guessed that a future IPL superstar once needed a place to stay in Mumbai and found it through a family who later ended up watching their own son chase an Australian cap.

Indeed, Wadia is now preparing for his first appearance in Australian representative colours, facing Bangladesh in Darwin from Thursday, and he's aware the coming season will test him differently now that opponents know what to expect from him.

"People will know me now, they will know my skills and look to counter that. It is up to me to find a way to be up for that and come out on top," he said.

"Ultimately, I want to play cricket for Australia. That is the goal, that is why I came here, to play at the highest level."

What makes this story compelling isn't just the celebrity connection but how grounded Wadia's account of it feels. He isn't leaning on the Pandya link as a shortcut; he's built his own path through club cricket, an academy program, and a proper Big Bash debut, all while staying appreciative of the encouragement that came his way.

That kind of humility, paired with a clear, ambitious goal of ultimately playing for Australia, suggests he understands exactly what it will take to sustain his rise now that the element of surprise is gone.

title: Chelsea welcome back Mudryk as four-year ban rescinded; Ukrainian winger set for Asia tour return
description: Chelsea have confirmed that Mykhailo Mudryk will head to Asia to join the club's pre-season tour after being cleared to return to football.Mudryk has been cleared to return to professional football, h...
fullText:
Chelsea have confirmed that Mykhailo Mudryk will head to Asia to join the club's pre-season tour after being cleared to return to football.

Mudryk has been cleared to return to professional football, having been suspended since November 2024 after a banned substance was found in a drugs test.

The Ukrainian has denied any intentional wrongdoing and has now been cleared to return with immediate effect, following an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS)

Chelsea are now ready to re-integrate the 25-year-old into the squad, confirming he will link up with the squad inAsia for pre-season.

“We know how much this opportunity to return means to him. Our focus now is on supporting Misha’s reintegration into the squad and helping him resume his career,"Chelsea said in a statement.

"Everyone at the Club now looks forward to helping Misha return to full fitness, back into the squad and back onto the pitch”.

Mudryk alsoreleased a statement, expressing his relief that his four-year ban has been rescinded and expressing his gratitude to the support he has received during the case.

He underlined his excitement to return to the pitch after 'the most difficult period' of his career.

“After a long battle, the four-year ban that was imposed on me has been rescinded and I am free to resume my career with immediate effect. I am grateful that this process has reached a conclusion, that I have been cleared to return to football and that I can now look ahead to my future.

"This has been the most difficult period of my career. As I have always maintained from the outset of this case, I have never knowingly or intentionally taken any banned substance. My commitment to competing fairly and representing my club and country with professionalism and integrity has always been important to me.

"I would like to thank my family and friends for their support and belief throughout this period. I also want to express my deep gratitude to everyone at Chelsea FC, my teammates and the Chelsea supporters who have been with me throughout. I would also like to thank my legal team and others who assisted for their tireless work on my case.

"My focus now is on returning to football, working hard every day, and making a positive contribution on the pitch. Thank you to everyone who continued to believe in me. I look forward to the next chapter of my career”.

title: FC Barcelona Coach Flick Speaks On Potential Ferran Torres Exit
description: FC Barcelona coach Hansi Flick spoke about Ferran Torres' potential exit after their side lost on penalties to Birmingham City on Friday night.
fullText:
FC Barcelona coach Hansi Flick spoke about Ferran Torres' potential exit after their side lost on penalties to Birmingham City on Friday night.

“I spoke with him during the World Cup, but now he is on holiday, he is important for us,” Flick insisted.

As implied, Ferran didn’t feature in the 2-2 friendly draw in England, where young Egyptian hopeful Hamza Abdelkarim bagged both of the Blaugrana’s goals.

Like many World Cup stars in the squad, he is still on holiday and should link up with the rest of his club teammates in the coming weeks.

Even before netting Spain’s winning extra time goal in the final against Argentina, however, to seal a second World Cup title, Ferran had already been linked with a potential move away from the Spotify Camp Nou.

Once more, his former Spain boss Luis Enrique - like he did with Dro Fernandez - attempted to convince Ferran that his future lies at the Parc des Princes.

Already, we’ve seen reports of the 26-year-old being in “advanced talks” with the Qatari-owned Champions League holders.

Ferran’s contract expires in under a year from now on June 30, 2027, meaning that this is the last summer to earn a reasonable transfer fee for him.

Ideally, in any potential sale, Barça would like to recoup a good portion of the $63.5 million (€55 million) they agreed to pay Manchester City for him in late 2021.

It’s certainly true that Ferran’s stock will have risen since his exploits in the United States, where his strike against Lionel Messi’s nation was the only one he managed across the FIFA-held tournament amid acting as a back up to Mikel Oyarzabal.

Yet ideally the Catalans would like to keep Torres, who netted 16 goals performing a similar function for Robert Lewandowski in 2025/2026, as Flick’s men retained the La Liga title.

Failed pursuits for the likes of Julian Alvarez and Junior Kroupi would leave the defending Spanish champions seriously short-staffed up front if Torres were to walk.

Lewandowski has since departed to the Chicago Fire after his own contract expired, while Hamza Abdelkarim might not yet be ready for regular time in the elite.

When Ferran is back and FC Barcelona are ready to make their season debut against Elche on August 23rd, we’ll see who Flick fancies with Dani Olmo another option as a false ‘9’. That’s if Ferran is still around.

title: Real Madrid want to sign a ‘world class’ centre-back this summer – report
description: Real Madrid are staring at their first pre-season friendly against Fiorentina, and Jose Mourinho already stares at a situation where not a single first-team defender is available.While the new signing...
fullText:
Real Madrid are staring at their first pre-season friendly against Fiorentina, and Jose Mourinho already stares at a situation where not a single first-team defender is available.

While the new signing Ibrahima Konate is on vacation, Antonio Rudiger is still not back up to speed to feature yet. Dean Huijsen is suffering from discomfort, Raul Asencio is injured and Eder Militao is far from returning from his long-term injury.

At this point, it is thus clear as daylight to Jose Mourinho that a new centre-back is the need of the hour, and the manager is thus pushing for the signing.

As relayed by MARCA in a recent report, Real Madrid want to sign a world-class centre-back this summer and see it as an absolute priority. The manager sees his project as ‘crying out’ for a new defender to add depth.

Asencio must leave for a new signing. (Photo by Fran Santiago/Getty Images)

For one player to arrive, however, one must depart and the club are already working on sealing the exit of Raul Asencio to free up the needed space.

Even the academy graduate’s recent injury does not change the club’s stance and they still plan on selling him, although they know well that it will be more complicated with him suffering a setback. August will be crucial on that front.

Jose Mourinho has never been one to count heavily on academy stars, but he will likely be forced to do so in Real Madrid’s upcoming preseason friendly. There are, after all, good talents in La Fabrica who can be reliable backups.

Bastoni is a top transfer target. (Photo by Tullio M. Puglia/Getty Images)

Lamini Fati and Joan Martinez are two of the most promising names in the academy who will likely even feature in the team’s upcoming games.

While a new signing will indeed be prioritised, Martinez and Fati have a big chance to prove a point and earn a place in Jose Mourinho’s dynamics for next season.

In terms of new signings, Inter Milan’s Alessandro Bastoni has emerged as the top transfer target in recent weeks, although it will prove to be another expensive affair. The club, however, appear to be confident of having the economic freedom to pull off the deal.

title: South Korea baseball league cancels two games over heatwave
description: South Korea's baseball league cancelled two professional games Saturday to ensure the safety of players and fans in a heatwave."The decision was made with the safety and health of spectators and players as the top priority," it said, adding that the games would be rescheduled.
fullText:
South Korea's baseball league cancelled two professional games Saturday to ensure the safety of players and fans in a heatwave.

The highest level of heat warning --  issued when temperatures are forecast to reach at least 39C -- has been in effect since Friday in Busan and Changwon, where the games had been scheduled.

Saturday's games between Samsung and Lotte in Busan and KIA and NC in Changwon were cancelled, the Korea Baseball Organization said in a statement.

"Severe heatwave warnings have been in effect for the Changwon and Busan areas since yesterday," it said.

"The decision was made with the safety and health of spectators and players as the top priority," it said, adding that the games would be rescheduled.

Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.

Temperatures topped 40C in South Korea's southeastern city of Yangsan for a fourth straight day on Saturday, hitting a record 41.6C.

A reading of 42C in Yangsan would mark the highest recorded under South Korea's modern weather observation system, including automatic weather stations, according to Seoul's Yonhap news agency.

Interior ministry data showed 13 people had died among 1,701 who suffered illnesses from heat-related causes in the first seven months of this year.

South Korea issued its first-ever emergency heatwave alert in July, advising people to avoid outdoor activities and stay cool under a new warning system.

title: A Manchester City star is determined to prove the doubters wrong and be the player he always has been
description: Phil Foden signed a contract extension with Manchester City which runs until the summer of 2030 ahead of City’s preseason tour of Asia. It is clear that the FA Cup and Carabao Cup holders are firmly...
fullText:
Phil Foden signed a contract extension with Manchester City which runs until the summer of 2030 ahead of City’s preseason tour of Asia. It is clear that the FA Cup and Carabao Cup holders are firmly backing Foden to get back to his dominant best. The past two seasons haven’t gone to plan for Fode. However, Foden did show signs during the first half of last season that his scintillating and damaging form does remain. Although, the second half of the season did see Foden’s firm drop off. In a new interview, Foden has stated that he is ready to prove the doubters wrong next season. Phil Foden seems determined to make a big impact for Enzo Maresca’s side.

In an in-depth interview with Simon Bajkowski for The Manchester Evening News, Phil Foden spoke about why his form dropped off during the second half of the 2025-26 season. Foden was one of Manchester City’s best players during the early stages of last season. His move into midfield had paid off and he looked at home in his new role. However, that form didn’t hold and Foden fell down the pecking order in Pep Guardiola’s final season as Manchester City manager.

Speaking on what occurred last season, Foden explained: “It was like a season of two halves for me. I think the first half of it was really good. I performed quite well and in the second half I couldn’t really get going and then get a lot of game time.”

“Obviously I’m an adaptable player as well, so it doesn’t help sometimes when you’re changing a lot of positions and it’s hard to maintain the performance of one position, but sometimes it just happens. It’s football. People who were playing in front of me was performing very well as well. And sometimes that’s just the way it is.”

Ultimately, Phil Foden missed on selection in England’s 2026 World Cup squad after his form fell away last season. Also, Foden is determined to use the criticism of his performances over the past two seasons as motivation. He added: “You’ve got to take it with a pinch of salt and then just try and react and prove people wrong and that’s all you can do really. A fresh start now and hopefully that doesn’t happen again.”

Phil Foden is correct in his assessment that his form during the first half of last season was very good. It is a reminder of how damaging he can be as a player when he is in peak form. Unfortunately, the second half of last season didn’t go as well. But that is football, and it does seem like missing out on selection for the World Cup and the criticism of Foden’s performances for the last two seasons have lit a fire under him. A hungry and motivated Phil Foden could be a nightmare for the opponents of Manchester City to contend with.

It is also clear that Manchester City will do all they can to help Phil Foden return to his best. The contract extension they granted the England international is a big indication of this. The City hierarchy have not, and will not, give up on Foden. He is too good a player for this to occur and he is too special to Manchester City as a club to be cast aside. Foden has come out the others side of two difficult seasons. City have maintained the faith in him and hopefully it is repaid throughout the 2026-27 season and beyond.

Phil Foden is motivated to use any criticism of his form over the past two seasons as fuel for his fire. Manchester City know that if Foden is in supreme form, they are a different beast for their opponents to contend with. A hungry, determined and motivated Phil Foden, entering the prime years of his career, could be one of the stars of the 2026-27 season. Manchester City and Foden himself are hoping that is exactly what transpires.

title: Barcelona star Gerard Martín outlines objectives after Birmingham friendly: ‘Our goal is to win everything’
description: Gerard Martin urged calm after FC Barcelona’s 2-2 draw with Birmingham City, followed by a 3-2 defeat on penalties, insisting the result was less important than the progress made during pre-season.T...
fullText:
Gerard Martin urged calm after FC Barcelona’s 2-2 draw with Birmingham City, followed by a 3-2 defeat on penalties, insisting the result was less important than the progress made during pre-season.

The defender, who started the match at St. Andrew’s Stadium, acknowledged that Birmingham City’s superior fitness showed at times but believes Barcelona produced plenty of encouraging moments.

“They have more match fitness than we do. We’re only just starting, so that’s normal. But I also think we had many good moments. We’re a very young team right now, and we should be happy with what we’ve done.”

Martin also spoke positively about partnering Andreas Christensen in central defence, a pairing that had few opportunities to develop last season.

“Last year we didn’t get many chances to play together, but he’s a great player and it’s always enjoyable playing alongside him,” he noted.

Gerard Martin started alongside Christensen in defence. (Photo by Alex Caparros/Getty Images)

The left-footed defender reserved special praise for the academy and youth players who have joined the first team during pre-season.

After all, Hamza Abdelkarim starred for Barcelona with a brace last night while Ebrima Tunkara also showcased his immense potential.

According to Martin, the youngsters have handled themselves well despite facing a physically demanding opponent.

“We’ve competed really well, and I’m very happy with all of them.”

He admitted that this pre-season has felt unusual due to the absence of many senior internationals.

“It’s a bit of a strange preparation because there aren’t many of our usual teammates here.”

Asked whether he considers himself a first-choice player heading into the new campaign, Martin made it clear that places must be earned every day.

“You have to prove yourself in every training session and every match. I’ll keep fighting to make sure that’s the case.”

Ready to fight for his place. (Photo by George Wood/Getty Images)

The defender also outlined the squad’s objectives for the season, stressing that Barcelona want to compete for every available trophy.

“Our goal is to win everything. We have a special desire to win the Champions League, but we also want to win every other competition.”

Martin finished by praising the conditions at St. George’s Park, saying the facilities and cooler weather have made preparation easier than training in the summer heat of Barcelona.

“The facilities are excellent, and it’s much more comfortable training here than in Barcelona. You don’t have to deal with the intense heat.”

title: How to watch Tour de France Femmes 2026: TV channel, highlights and streaming online
description: All you need to know about how to watch this year’s Tour de France Femmes
fullText:
The Tour de France Femmes begins on Saturday with possibly the most difficult route yet for women’s cycling’s flagship race.

This year the peloton will tackle the infamous Mont Ventoux on a gruelling stage seven, the queen stage of the nine-day race, but the battle for the general classification could go right down to the wire with four summits of the Col d’Eze, outside Nice, crammed into less than 100km in an explosive final stage.

Dutchwoman and 2023 champion Demi Vollering is arguably the favourite to regain her crown but will face fierce competition from reigning champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot, who has had a mixed season but with everything building towards her title defence, and 2024 winner Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, who has finished on the podium in every edition.

Elsewhere Britain’s Zoe Backstedt is one of the favourites to take a maiden stage win on stage four’s individual time trial, as the 21-year-old makes her Tour de France debut.

Here’s everything you need to know to watch the race.

The Tour de France Femmes begins in Lausanne on Saturday 1 August, running for nine stages until the finish line in Nice on Sunday 9 August.

Viewers in the UK can watch the race on TNT Sports and HBO Max. A subscription starts from £25.99 per month for an annual subscription, or £30.99 if paid monthly. This year there is no free-to-air coverage of the Tour de France Femmes.

Chief among the contenders is the Netherlands’ Demi Vollering, who won this race in 2023 and won the Giro d’Italia in June to complete the full set of Grand Tour wins. The European champion is in stunning form, having won Liege-Bastogne-Liege and the Tour of Flanders among other races in a glittering Classics campaign before that recent Giro triumph. Her FDJ Suez-United team is assembled entirely around her, with the likes of French climber Evita Muzic and this year’s Paris-Roubaix champion Franziska Koch excellent lieutenants.

Defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot has had a middling season so far; second at the Tour of Flanders and third place at Paris-Roubaix were the highlights but her results have otherwise been average, including a rather anonymous showing at the Vuelta Femenina. But she has been open about building her season entirely towards the Tour and having cemented her triumph on the Col de la Madeleine last year the inclusion of Mont Ventoux will suit her, although the individual time trial is much better suited to Vollering than the Frenchwoman.

2024 champion Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney has been on the podium of every edition and reliably brings her best to the Tour; her Canyon-SRAM squad is a strong one, too, including former Giro d’Italia podium finisher Antonia Niedermaier, who will provide support in the mountains. But although she has been putting in significant time on the TT bike the time trial does not play to her strengths, and she has not looked able to match Vollering on the climbs so far this year.

Young Spanish prodigy Paula Blasi blew away the field at this year’s Vuelta Femenina and will be co-leader for UAE Team L'IMAD alongside two-time Giro winner Elisa Longo Borghini, with the team able to play multiple cards. Longo Borghini has had a difficult year hampered by illness but is the more natural leader of the team; the squad will likely have to balance the pair’s competing interests, particularly if Blasi arrives in the same barnstorming form as she displayed in Spain, where she was particularly impressive on the toughest climbs - which bodes well for Mont Ventoux. UAE also have Maeva Squiban, who won two stages last year, and Dominika Wlodarczyk, who finished fourth last year.

Movistar leader Marlen Reusser has had a run of bad luck at the sport’s biggest races, including abandoning last year’s Tour with illness on stage one, and crashes and illness have held her back at points this season too. But she won her home race, the Tour de Suisse, earlier this summer and looks to be back at her best; the 34-year-old can climb with the best and as reigning time-trial world champion will expect to gain time on her rivals on stage four.

Finally, SD Worx-Protime will be led by Anna van der Breggen, a legend of the sport who may not be quite at her electric best but is certainly not far off it. Second at the Vuelta and third at the Giro, where she wore the maglia rosa for much of the race, indicate she remains a serious threat. High mountains like Mont Ventoux have always suited her and the ITT also plays in her favour.

"We are aware of the reports concerning Anthony Smith’s recent arrest. At this time, it would be inappropriate to comment on the allegations or speculate regarding facts that have yet to be fully established," Butlter wrote on Instagram.

"Like every individual, Anthony is entitled to the presumption of innocence and the due process protections afforded under our justice system. We respectfully ask that people avoid rushing to judgment based solely on initial reports, as they often do not reflect the complete facts or context.

"Our thoughts are with Anthony and his family as they navigate this difficult and deeply personal matter. We ask that their privacy be respected while the legal process runs its course.

"Out of respect for the ongoing proceedings, we will have no further comment at this time."

title: Intensity, smiles & Lewandowski - inside Liverpool training under Iraola
description: Liverpool's pre-season under Andoni Iraola is ramping up - and here is what we learned from the first open training session under their new boss.
fullText:
As Liverpool's first open training session under Andoni Iraola began, Robert Lewandowski was taking penalties in the background.

The session took place at the performance centre of Major League Soccer side Chicago Fire, where the 37-year-old Pole now plays.

Under gloomy skies, Lewandowski blazed a spot-kick over the bar as Fire's training session came to an end and Iraola's got under way.

Here is what we learned from Liverpool's session.

Liverpool's Jones argues with Szoboszlai after game

Earlier this week, a video was posted on social media of Dominik Szoboszlai and Curtis Jones - who has been linked with a move to Inter Milan - having a heated argument at the end of Liverpool's win over Wrexham on Wednesday.

Asked about the situation on Thursday, Szoboszlai played it down, insisting all the players "were in the same boat" in terms of wanting the best for the club and each other.

Regardless, Szoboszlai, Jones and Kostas Tsimikas, who was also in the clip, walked out together in good spirits, doing keepy-uppies and joking with each other right in front of the cameras.

The argument was understood to be related to the fact that Szoboszlai had given Tsimikas the captain's armband instead of Jones but, by Friday, it seemed to have settled.

A little bit of passion is never a bad thing in an elite sporting environment but, with the way footage can be captured from anyone inside a stadium, sometimes it is better to keep things behind closed doors.

It was far from ideal - and it served as a reminder for Iraola that he must appoint a vice-captain soon, with the vacancy open after Andy Robertson's departure.

Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai seem to have resolved their differences in training following a heated argument after their win against Wrexham 🤝 pic.twitter.com/66eHdCDcTE

— Match of the Day (@BBCMOTD) July 31, 2026

Record signing Alexander Isak also returned to Liverpool training this week.

He, Florian Wirtz and Ryan Gravenberch all missed the trip to New York, where Liverpool beat Wrexham 1-0 in their second pre-season fixture, but are expected to feature on Sunday against Leeds.

Jeremy Jacquet missed training but was in the gym as the club carefully manage his recovery from the shoulder injury he sustained in February.

The centre-back is a doubt for the weekend, despite Iraola suggesting earlier in the week that he would feature.

Joe Gomez, who has been ruled out for the start of the Premier League season, was also in the gym.

Once the warm-ups were done, the intensity in Iraola's drills was clear to see. He likes to get heavily involved and was particularly animated, using phrases like "play in possession" and "quicker, quicker" repeatedly.

There were celebrations between players whenever they scored in the mini-drills and the atmosphere was generally positive, with Iraola unafraid to step in and point out something, or discuss a player's position.

The squad then separated, with one group moving on to a smaller pitch for a nine-a-side match while another group worked on set-pieces with Iraola's assistants, Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper.

Wirtz was on corner duty, while Elphick even put on a bib to get involved.

Watching on was Mike Gordon, the Fenway Sports Group president, who is now overseeing Liverpool operations again. He is expected to be at the game on Sunday at Soldier Field in Chicago.

Liverpool had a team dinner on Thursday evening, with Iraola sharing a beer with the likes of Phil Thompson and Robbie Fowler after.

Thompson told BBC Sport they spoke about a number of things, from the season ahead to their families.

Iraola was not even born when former defender Thompson won the third of his three European Cups for Liverpool. But this was a sign of the new head coach recognising the legends of the club and the weight they still carry.

Iraola still has three weeks before his first Premier League game as Liverpool manager - but the seeds of his tenure are getting planted here in the Windy City.

title: Today’s Papers – Italy pays tribute to Baresi
description: Italian football is in mourning, and on Saturday its three great sports dailies handed their front pages over entirely to Franco Baresi, the Milan and Italy legend who died on Friday aged 66.According...
fullText:
Italian football is in mourning, and on Saturday its three great sports dailies handed their front pages over entirely to Franco Baresi, the Milan and Italy legend who died on Friday aged 66.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, the country has lost “a giant.” Beneath a photograph of Baresi lifting the European Cup, the pink paper leads with “Mio Capitano”, “My Captain”, recalling how the boy nicknamed “il Piscinin” grew into a colossus who won everything and stood by his Milan even through their relegation to Serie B.

Inside, tributes and interviews pour in from those who knew him best, among them former coach Fabio Capello, ex-team-mate Christian Panucci and Rossoneri great Gianni Rivera, alongside columns from the likes of Luigi Garlando and Beppe Bergomi.

Corriere dello Sport: Strikes a similar chord with “6 per sempre”, “Six forever”, a nod to the shirt number Milan retired in his honour. Under the line “Addio capitano,” the paper hails “elegance become legend” and reports that Italian football is “in tears,” having “lost a beat of our heart.”

It traces the arc of a life defined by 21 trophies, from the 1982 World Cup to three European Cups under Arrigo Sacchi and Fabio Capello, and carries the words of long-time defensive partner Alessandro Costacurta, who recalled how Baresi “knew how to lead you through his conduct.”

Turin’s Tuttosport keeps it simple: “Un capitano,” above the dates 1960-2026 and another image of Baresi and the European Cup. Its tributes reach beyond the trophies to the moments that defined the man, the courage of his tearful stand at Pasadena in the 1994 World Cup final, and the 39 red roses he laid in memory of the Heysel victims, “from a champion of humanity.”

The papers also carry the details of a nation’s farewell. Baresi’s funeral will be held on Tuesday 4 August at 11am at the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio in Milan, with the Rossoneri squad unable to attend as they are away on their pre-season tour. FIGC president Giovanni Malagò has ordered a minute’s silence before every friendly played in Italy this weekend.

title: Foden aims to repay Man City faith in fresh start
description: Manchester City midfielder Phil Foden is aiming to "repay" the faith shown to him by the club as he looks forward to a "fresh start" under new boss Enzo Maresca.
fullText:
Manchester City midfielder Phil Foden is aiming to "repay" the faith shown in him by the club as he aims for a "fresh start" under new manager Enzo Maresca.

The 26-year-old scored 19 goals as City won the Premier League in 2023-24 and was named the Professional Footballers' Association player of the year and the league's player of the season.

However, he has not managed to hit those heights in the past two seasons - scoring 10 times last term, but failing to net in his past 31 appearances for club and country.

Despite his struggles, Foden was offered a new contract by City and signed a four-year deal last month to keep him at Etihad Stadium until 2030.

"It has made me feel relaxed and I can just concentrate on being the best version of me and give back to the football club for them trusting in me," Foden said.

"It is nice to see the support from the club and obviously it means a lot.

"It's about time I try and repay them and give back to the club."

Foden was given his first-team debut as a 17-year-old by former manager Pep Guardiola and has gone on to make 369 appearances for City, winning six Premier League titles, one Champions League and two FA Cups.

Guardiola left at the end of last season and Italian Maresca was named as his replacement, returning to the club where he previously worked in the academy and as first-team assistant.

Asked how he was feeling this summer, academy product Foden said: "Very good - a fresh start, a new manager and up to now, really enjoying it.

"It is very strange but I know Enzo from before, so that also helps. I know him quite well and what [he] is about.

"That has definitely helped, to have that relationship with him."

Foden signs new four-year Man City contract

Foden started for England in their 2024 European Championship final defeat by Spain but missed out on a place in Thomas Tuchel's squad for the 2026 World Cup.

The Three Lions reached the semi-finals of the tournament before losing 2-1 to Argentina, and Foden said it was hard watching them walk out for the national anthem before games.

Foden said Maresca had checked in with him after he was left out of Tuchel's squad.

Foden said: "He [Maresca] reached out just after to see if it was OK, which was very nice of him, to show us this character and the person he is.

"He cares about everyone and wants to have a good relationship with the team."

Foden struggled last season with a combination of off-field issues and an ankle injury, but says he is now "fully fit".

Asked about Foden's role in the team, Maresca said: "Phil is very important, like the rest. Knowing Phil from years ago, I know how good he is.

"It is my duty to help him be the Phil we all want.

"First of all, to be happy and enjoy football is most important. If he feels good, he can help us win titles."

Maresca will take charge of City for the first time in Saturday's friendly against Inter Milan in Hong Kong.

Despite losing the experience and knowhow of Guardiola, captain Bernardo Silva and England defender John Stones, Foden feels City can achieve "amazing things" next season.

Speaking at the club's new Puma away kit launch in Hong Kong, Foden said: "I think we can win everything, but it's obviously hard. We have still got an unbelievable team."

title: Ditcheva outclasses Kielholtz on return from injury
description: Dakota Ditcheva outclasses Denise Kielholtz as the Briton marks her return from injury with a comfortable win by unanimous decision at PFL New York.
fullText:
Dakota Ditcheva outclassed Denise Kielholtz as the Briton marked her return from injury with a comfortable win by unanimous decision at PFL New York.

Ditcheva, who had not fought since breaking her left hand just over a year ago, extended the unbeaten start to her career to 16 fights.

The win for Ditcheva, who triumphed in the PFL flyweight tournament in 2024, was a timely reminder to fans of why she is one of Britain's most talented and exciting fighters.

Although Ditcheva could not add to her 12 career knockouts - nine of which have come in the first round - she outstruck Dutch fighter Kielholtz 102-64.

Ditcheva's win cements her status as one of the biggest stars in the PFL just days after the organisation's merge with Most Valuable Promotions (MVP), while MVP co-founder Jake Paul was cage-side to watch the fights at the UBS Arena.

Ditcheva, 28, has had a frustrating year after her return was delayed in February when she suffered an injury to her opposite hand.

But she displayed her trademark confidence during her walkout as she sported a relaxed smile, before quickly finding her groove after the opening bell.

Using her superior height to her advantage, Ditcheva kept the 37-year-old Kielholtz at bay for the majority of the contest with a number of rangy kicks.

Ditcheva did some of her best work with her jab, while a number of knees and kicks to the body hurt Kielholtz at the start of the second round.

Kielholtz, who had won her past three fights before this bout, landed when she got in range but her punches often lacked the power of her British opponent.

Ditcheva's striking is widely regarded as her most dangerous asset, but she also showcased her grappling with six successful takedowns, leaving little doubt as to who had won.

The Briton did not give a post-fight interview but said pre-fight she is "enjoying her career" in the PFL, and "doesn't know" if she'll ever fight in the UFC.

Ditcheva also hinted at a future boxing bout, with MVP's merge with the PFL opening the door to potential opportunities.

MVP has invested heavily in women's boxing over the past five years and boasts an impressive stable of world champions, including Britons Caroline Dubois and Chantelle Cameron.

In the main event, Russia's Usman Nurmagomedov knocked out America's Archie Colgan in the first round to retain his PFL lightweight title.

Nurmagomedov, 28, rocked Colgan with a high kick, before finishing the contest with an uppercut to keep his undefeated record intact.

The victory was the 22nd of Nurmagomedov's career as he made the second defence of his PFL belt.

Nurmagomedov's win marked his sixth world title defence in total after the Bellator title was rebranded by the PFL in 2025.

Following victory, Nurmagomedov paid tribute to training partner and UFC welterweight champion Islam Makhachev.

"This is from sparring with UFC legend and champion Islam Makhachev, that's how you can improve," said Nurmagomedov.

"Only one guy in the world pushes harder than me - Makhachev. That's why I follow him."

title: Is building a new stadium a way around spending rules?
description: Spurs only just avoided Premier League relegation last season, but off the pitch they are thriving. So is building a new stadium a good way around spending rules?
fullText:
Tottenham fans will want to put last season behind them.

There was another managerial sacking, a spate of injuries to key players, and a nervy 90 minutes on the final day of the season as the ninth-richest club in the world, external narrowly avoided relegation from the Premier League.

A 17th-place finish for the second year running will be cause for concern, to say the least.

Off the pitch though it's a different story. Tottenham's finances, despite the team's poor form, are looking very rosy indeed. This is largely down to their new stadium and the huge revenues it brings.

So what can other clubs learn from their stadium success story? And is building a new home - or renovating an old one - the best way to balance the books?

We'll get to complying with financial rules in a moment, but first let's start by looking at how much a club like Tottenham are making on matchdays.

"Spurs' matchday income has increased from £45m in 2016-17, the season they left White Hart Lane, to £126m in 2024-25," explains football finance expert Kieran Maguire.

"So you've less than doubled the size of the stadium and yet the matchday revenue is up by two and a half times.

"What Spurs have done is they've created a welcoming environment. So if people are spending an extra 40 to 50 minutes in the stadium itself they're not just spending time - more importantly they're spending money."

Spurs can also host up to 30 non-football events a year at full capacity which is proving to be very beneficial.

Along with major concerts, the club has also hosted NFL games and boxing world title fights - including Anthony Joshua's heavyweight bout with Oleksandr Usyk in 2021. It's also been the venue for rugby union's Saracens hosting Harlequins in the London derby since 2023.

All of this brings in extra commercial revenue - which jumped from £73m in 2016-17 to £277m in 2024-25.

The extra income means the club can then invest 

This summer the Premier League is replacing its profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) with a new financial framework centred on squad-cost ratio (SCR) and sustainability and systemic resilience (SSR).

Put simply, SCR is designed to cap a club's total spending on its playing squad as a direct percentage of its overall revenue.

Club costs like player wages, transfer amortisation - spreading a transfer fee across the length of a player's contract for accounting purposes - and agent fees all get taken into account.

Crucially though, stadium infrastructure costs are not included in the SCR calculation.

"In the case of Spurs, their infrastructure costs are around £70m a year - but those are excluded." says Maguire. "Any money that you invest in stadiums is completely ring-fenced and excluded from your ability to invest in players.

"There's a separate issue in that stadiums do cost a lot of money. But Spurs borrowed from banks at spectacularly cheap interest rates."

In other words, for Spurs the pluses of building a new expensive stadium far outweigh the negatives, at least from a financial perspective.

"In order to be competitive, you need to have a significant increase in matchday income," says Maguire.

"You could only do that from either increasing prices, which isn't going to go down well, or increasing the size of the stadium with a greater proportion of the tickets going to the non-season ticket fanbase."

Like Tottenham, Everton and West Ham have also moved to new stadiums - which while financially attractive in the long-term, hasn't always gone down well with fans.

Other Premier League clubs are looking at their options. Should they stay or go?

Renovation is the cheaper route, but the problem then is where do the team play if they have to move out while building takes place?

The obvious barrier to moving to a new stadium is the huge cost - but there's also the concern from fans that they'll lose something by leaving their historical home.

It is clear Sir Jim Ratcliffe wants a new stadium to be the statement around his involvement at Manchester United.

Yet it is equally clear a new build, with a 100,000 capacity and a significant number of corporate areas, would generate far more than United get on a matchday now, which will help drive revenues and improve the senior squad.

There are other financial aspects though, which few will consider in the bigger picture.

The initial plans unveiled by Ratcliffe in March 2025 featured a huge canopy. That in itself will be costly, but in theory the overhang and what is underneath it will be in United's footprint - and the club will be responsible for it. Will the expense be worth the 'look'?

Construction could - in part - take place off site and be shipped in if club officials are to be believed. That is likely to cost less than doing all the work in Old Trafford.

And then having a new build where it is, down the road from their current ground, deals with the potentially thorny problem about where United would play if Old Trafford was closed for a period.

None of Manchester City, Liverpool or Everton's grounds are ideal from a security perspective. All have a lower capacity than Old Trafford and all would cost a lot to hire, even if it was desirable.

United's current plans mean they can simply move from one stadium to another.

For Newcastle, a club which this summer has effectively had to sell some of its best players in order to stay within the financial rules, the argument over moving to a new purpose-built stadium is compelling.

"For the 2024-25 season Newcastle's matchday income was £52m. Manchester United's was £160m, Arsenal's £154m, Spurs' was £126m.

"If you're £100m behind your competitors, the only way to address that is either to be super smart or to charge more money for the product.

"How can Newcastle increase the yield per fan and still be loyal to the Gallowgate hardcore? You need to be able to offer a different product and St James' Park wasn't built for a corporate audience."

Will the fans back a move though?

Newcastle supporter Charlotte Robson has mixed feelings.

"I think we can host gigs at St James' Park but probably not on the scale of Spurs or West Ham's London Stadium.

"I don't think it would be stupid to move from the ground but I think there is so much identity for Newcastle fans who are attached to St James' Park that it would break a lot of hearts to move the ground in any significant way."

Along with increased matchday revenue, clubs weighing up whether to move will also hope to make more commercial revenue - but Maguire is cautious.

"Spurs have got the advantage that they're in London - a huge tourist trap. They are also a club with a global fanbase, so it works there.

"Is that going to work elsewhere in the country where you've got a more localised fanbase and where there is resistance to putting up prices for tickets? Then it becomes more challenging.

"We have seen a substantial increase in the costs of putting stadiums together, but there still seems to be an appetite for it."

title: Silicon Valley loves young founders. Until it doesn't
description: AI tools have democratized the opportunity to build, shortening the timelines of success and enabling more young people to start successful companies without stepping foot inside a Big Tech company.
fullText:
For Arlan Rakhmetzhanov, 19, there is no middle ground. Either he builds a company as valuable as Google, he says, or he fails and ends up on the streets. He started coding at 15 in his native Kazakhstan, completed a couple of summer programs in San Francisco, and cold-DM’ed every Y Combinator founder he could find on LinkedIn until one gave him an angel check for his first company at age 17.

That company, now the YC-backed Nozomio, is an API index for AI agents — a tool that helps AI agents find and use software services — and has raised more than $6 million in funding to date. “I either win or lose, and a lot of young founders have the same mindset,” he told TechCrunch. “They just want to win.”

Young founders like Rakhmetzhanov are building under a new set of pressures. Investors are throwing more capital at them, yet the expectation to hit that “north star” milestone — the one big number investors are chasing — hasn’t relaxed, and every misstep along the way is now publicly dissected on social media.

While Silicon Valley VCs have always famously loved backing young college dropout founders, they preferred to see them paired with technical founders, or at least to have some experience — ideally with a FAANG company (Meta, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Google) — on their résumés. In many ways, that is still very true. But AI tools have democratized the opportunity to build, shortening the timelines of success and enabling more young people to start successful companies without stepping foot inside a Big Tech company.

Pranjali Awasthi, 19, is an example of that. She dropped out of high school to launch an AI startup, then attended Georgia Tech before dropping out of that, too, to launch Slashy, a YC-backed startup that bills itself as the “Cursor for emails” and helps consumers manage their email inboxes. After more than a year running that company, she recently announced she’s now building yet a new startup currently in stealth.

When she was younger, around 14 or 15, she recalled, investors whom she would pitch often asked why she was looking to build a company. “It’s gotten more normal now,” she said, “post-18.”

It seems more than ever, investors look to founders like Awasthi, whose experiences can be traced through “GitHub activity, open-source contributions, communities they’ve already built, and familiarity with all the latest tools in AI,” Ashley Smith, a general partner at the early-stage firm Vermilion, told TechCrunch. “A lot of young developers learn how to build software through contributing to open-source projects or toying around with the latest AI tooling,” she explained. “They have more time to do that while in college or younger than someone with a full-time job and a mortgage.”

Smith said a “meaningful” share of her portfolio consists of companies founded by those under 30, with a handful even younger than 21, she said, adding that she’s “clearly not skeptical of youth.”

“What they lack in experience, they make up for in excitement to experiment and lack of fear,” she continued.

But she admits the market has become more merciless. “It doesn’t give you room to learn slowly anymore,” she said. There are more funding opportunities than ever, regardless of age — accelerators, incubators, pre-seed funds. But that money comes with strings attached: Founders like Rakhmetzhanov and Awasthi, flush with millions in cash, are expected to deliver growth in months, not years.

“The forgiveness that used to exist at an early stage and the assumption you’d iterate your way to product-market fit doesn’t exist right now,” Smith continued. “Everyone is looking for the next Cursor, even though that growth trajectory is an outlier, not the norm.”

For many founders — especially those building in public — the relentless strain to succeed can lead to murky ethical territory, or even predatory deal terms, since younger founders are often too new to the game to know what’s standard, yet ambitious enough to chase growth at all costs. To keep up, revenue numbers start to look inflated, while content creation for social media starts to crowd out writing good code. The excessive posturing is perhaps inevitable, since getting attention is now harder than ever in a crowded AI market.

It’s all about who can convince “the most people [they] are smarter than everyone else in the space,” Smith said, “and make the most noise about it.”

“In 2004, you could quietly iterate for years without anyone watching,” Awasthi added. “Now there is this constant ambient pressure from LinkedIn and Twitter where every raise, every milestone, every pivot is public.”

That means some young founders aren’t just worried about hitting competitive revenue marks or funding valuations — they’re also under pressure to perform the appearance of being a successful founder. That pressure has always existed in startup culture, but founders say it’s grown more extreme. “If you’re a startup and you’re competing in a market, usually you worry about incumbents,” Timothy Chen, an investor at Essence Ventures, told TechCrunch. “Now you worry about your neighbors.”

For example, “everybody’s doing shiny, good-looking launch videos,” he noted. “It wasn’t even a thing three years ago.” The trend was popularized by Cluely founder Roy Lee, now around age 22, whose startup initially promised to help students cheat on exams — a premise that dazzled investors like Andreessen Horowitz and helped the company raise $20 million.

Though Cluely is now more of a note-taking tool, Lee became a face of young Silicon Valley talent. “The pressure is coming from, ‘I need to show off much better, quick,’” Chen continued.

Not hitting the bar has bred new anxiety. “When Zuck was building Facebook, there wasn’t this huge negative social ecosystem,” Aidan Guo, 20, told TechCrunch. He’s the co-founder of the AI desktop assistant startup Attention Engineering, which has raised around $1.6 million in funding to date.

Much of the strain, as he describes it, is self-imposed. “You already have a constant fear of failure on your mind. You have to steer the ship and learn all these things as you go. And everything can always go wrong at once,” he continued. “And then you have all these people piling on anything you do wrong. I think people need to be more empathetic.”

Amid all that pressure, Awasthi takes a page from the old days. “If you focus your time on what needs to get done, it’s not too hard,” she said.

“The best product that stays active and talks to customers wins,” Rakhmetzhanov added.

In the end, all the founders are describing the same thing: The fundamentals of a good startup haven’t changed — “conviction, intellectual honesty, and obsession with the customer,” as Smith put it. None of that has anything to do with age.

title: Google plans to exempt sanctioned nations from Android developer verification
description: Someone in Cuba or Iran can keep installing APKs with no new restrictions, but devs will suffer.
fullText:
We are a month away from the initial rollout of Google’s Android developer verification system, and the company contends this policy does not impinge on the platform’s open nature. Still, the restrictions will be a big change, and there are still some unanswered questions. An issue that has come up repeatedly in the run-up to verification is what will happen to devs who can’t verify because of where they live. It turns out that Google has a cryptic answer for that buried in an FAQ.

Developer verification will soon block the installation of apps from unverified developers on any Android device running Google services, which is functionally all Android phones outside Russia and China. Developers who want to keep releasing software, even if it’s not in the Play Store, have to provide Google with their ID and pay a small fee.

But what if you’re an Android developer living in a sanctioned nation? Currently, the US sanction list includes Iran, Cuba, North Korea, and occupied areas of Ukraine. Given the current uncertain state of US foreign policy, that list could change in the future. Google doing any business with developers in those places is a thorny issue, and it seems like the company has decided to just leave them hanging.

A rather lengthy FAQ a few levels deep on the Google developer site addresses various issues around dev verification. Smack in the middle is this:

How does this program impact developers in sanctioned countries? Devices in sanctioned countries will be excluded from Android developer verification checks. This allows any developer to continue distributing apps in these regions without verification, though users there won’t benefit from the enhanced security benefits of the program.

The wording is bizarre because the answer doesn’t directly address the most important question—it dodges it. The vague FAQ appears to suggest that these developers won’t be able to verify, but that’s OK because phones in their countries won’t require that. But this comes with a real downside for those people.

A Google spokesperson has expanded on the FAQ and confirmed to Ars that people living in sanctioned nations will not be allowed to go through the verification process. That means they will not be able to effectively distribute software through any channel internationally.

Today, someone making an app in, say, Cuba can distribute it freely around the world, as well as at home. Anyone can install it and see their work in action after tapping through a few sideloading alerts. In the coming months, that will no longer be the case. These unverified apps will only be easily installable in the sanctioned countries where verification doesn’t exist.

Earlier this year, Google clarified its plans for the “advanced flow” to bypass developer verification. It requires a bunch of steps, scary warnings, and a 24-hour wait. That gives tech-savvy folks a way to get around the new restrictions, but most people won’t know such an option even exists. Verification will necessarily create a two-tiered system of apps: verified ones that anyone can install and unverified apps that almost no one can install. Google says this change is necessary to combat scam apps.

Paradoxically, the situation in sanctioned nations will actually provide more app freedom. And these are Google-certified phones at issue here. In places like Cuba and Iran, most phones are Android devices with full Google certification because they’re imported from other places where Google officially operates. So Google is essentially acknowledging in this FAQ that its mobile services are being used and nominally supported in these places.

Google probably sees this as a legal tightrope. It can’t engage with developers in these places to verify them, but it seems determined to move forward with developer verification. The solution, apparently, is to leave devs in these regions behind—no verification, but no enforcement, either. The rest of us will have a more restricted app experience as users, but most developers around the world will be able to distribute their software anywhere as long as they verify. Sanctioned developers, meanwhile, will be in a second-tier bubble. Google has therefore tied the ability to distribute Android apps to the whims of the US Treasury Department, which maintains and enforces economic sanctions.

Currently, Google plans to activate the verification restrictions on September 30 in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. The program is expected to expand globally in 2027.

title: AI doesn't generate working products, that's still your job
description: AI has dramatically accelerated the path to a first working version. It has not shortened the distance between a first working version and something production-grade.
fullText:
Building software has never felt this accessible. You describe an idea in plain English, and within minutes, a working prototype appears on your screen. It has a UI. It connects to a database. It does the thing you imagined. For someone who has never written a line of code, that moment feels like magic. For someone who has spent years wrestling with compilers and stack traces, it's genuinely astonishing.

The prototype runs on your laptop. It breaks under load. It has no error handling. You find out that it may be leaking your API tokens. The data model made sense for the demo but falls apart the moment you add a second user. The authentication is held together with assumptions. There's a nagging worry whether everything is secure. You want to deploy it, and suddenly you're staring at a chasm between "this works" and "this is ready."

Software engineers have always been able to get something running quickly. What took time was everything else: designing systems that hold up at scale, handling the cases users weren't supposed to encounter but inevitably do, building in observability so you know when things break, making deliberate decisions about data architecture that you'll regret less three years from now. None of that has changed. AI has dramatically accelerated the path to a first working version. It has not shortened the distance between a first working version and something production-grade.

The confusion arises because the feedback loop for the early part of the journey has become so fast and so rewarding. You ask, you receive, you see results. That cycle is genuinely exciting, and it creates the impression that the rest of software development must be similarly compressed. It isn't. The hard problems of building software were never primarily about writing syntax. They were about judgment: what to build, how to structure it, what to defer, when to say no. That judgement is what turns a vibe-coder into a sculptor, and an artisan. It is also what differentiates a prototype from a production-grade system.

Predictably, the accessibility of AI-generated code has sparked a wave of new entrants to the industry who are questioning whether it still makes sense to learn computer science. If you can describe your way to a working application, why spend years studying algorithms, data structures, operating systems, and theory?

The value of a computer science education was never purely in the ability to produce code. It was in developing a mental model of how systems behave, how they fail, and why. That model is what allows you to look at AI-generated code and recognize that the query it wrote will cause a full table scan on a table with fifty million rows. It's what allows you to see that the caching strategy it proposed will create a race condition under concurrent load. It's what tells you that the architecture it suggested solves the problem you described but will make the next problem significantly harder.

Without that foundation, you are entirely dependent on the model's judgment. And models don't have judgment. They have pattern matching, with an eagerness to produce code that it believes matches your intent. They will confidently generate code that looks right, follows convention, and fails in production in ways that take days to diagnose if you don't know what you're looking for.

Now is arguably the best time in history to learn computer science, because the gap between understanding and output has collapsed. A student who genuinely grasps how a distributed system works can now build one in a fraction of the time it would have taken a decade ago.

The demand for engineers who can only write code mechanically, and who translates requirements into implementations line by line, are genuinely declining. That part of the job is being automated.

What's happening is a compression of the lower end of the productivity distribution and an expansion of the ceiling for those at the top. An experienced engineer using modern AI tools can move at a pace that would have been unimaginable five years ago. Not because the hard problems have disappeared, but because the mechanical work that consumed so much time and attention is largely handled. More hours in the day for the work that actually requires expertise.

The engineers who will be left behind are not those who lack AI skills. They're the ones who use AI as a substitute for understanding, who vibe-code their way through systems they can't reason about, and then find themselves unable to fix what breaks, unable to scale what grows, unable to explain what they built to anyone who needs to maintain it.

The shift required isn't about adopting a new set of tools. It's about operating at a higher level of abstraction while keeping your roots in the fundamentals. That combination is genuinely powerful and genuinely rare.

The engineers who will leapfrog their peers in the next few years are the ones who treat AI as a force multiplier on deep knowledge rather than a replacement for it. They understand what they're asking the model to produce. They review generated code with the same critical eye they'd apply to a junior engineer's pull request. They bring architectural thinking to the conversation, not just feature descriptions. They know when to push back on what the model suggests.

It's the old skill set, applied to a new context, with dramatically higher leverage.

The prototype is the easy part. The difference now is that everyone can see that clearly. What comes after the prototype is still hard, still requires real engineering judgment, and still separates the builders who ship reliable software from the ones who ship demos.

Learn the fundamentals. Then learn the new tools. In that order.
