title: Wales golden girls beat England in cycling duel
description: Wales golden girls Emma Finucane and Anna Morris win the Commonwealth Games battle of Britain by defeating English rivals in Glasgow.
fullText:
Wales golden girls Emma Finucane and Anna Morris won the Commonwealth Games battle of Britain by defeating England in Glasgow.

Finucane won her second gold in two nights as she eased to team sprint success against Sophie Capewell, while Morris beat Josie Knight in the 4,000m individual pursuit final.

There was further drama for Morris, who finished second in the scratch race just over an hour after her gold medal race before she was demoted to fifth.

With Rhian Edmunds picking up a surprise bronze in the sprint, Wales have won six medals on the opening two nights at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, three of them gold.

With Finucane and Morris about, there is set to be more success.

"These Games have been the highlight of my career alongside the Olympics," said Finucane.

"It's been amazing what we've achieved as such a small nation.

"We've had Anna winning today and pulled it through. I believe it's the passion and belief we have."

Finucane is working her way into the record books.

After adding individual sprint to team success, she became the first Welsh woman to win two golds at the same Commonwealth Games since athlete Kirsty Wade in 1986 in Edinburgh.

Based on this domination, there will be further podium finishes to come in Scotland, with Finucane still due to take part in the time trial and keirin in the next two days.

The 23-year-old from Carmarthen bossed this day from start to finish. In short, she was a class apart from the moment her bike hit the track.

In qualification, Finucane set a new Games record of 10.322 seconds and defeated reigning Commonwealth and Olympic champion Ellesse Andrews in the quarter-finals with ease.

Victory in an all-Welsh semi-final against Edmunds - who she had won team sprint gold alongside on opening night - followed to set up the Team GB final against Capewell.

The pair were part of the Great Britain team sprint squad that won gold at the Paris Olympics in 2024 and were now competing against each other.

Capewell had made the final after a controversial semi-final success against Malaysia's Nurul Mohammed Asri, who was disqualified in one of the races because of delaying race tactics.

Capewell eventually prevailed to make the final but it mattered little who Finucane would face as she sped to gold, with Edmunds also ending up on the podium.

"Today was a rollercoaster because qualifying first, you have that expectation of winning at the end of the day," said Finucane.

"There are so many riders you've got to get through and so many races to win to even make it to the final against Sophie.

"We had a great fight out there and I was so glad to cross the line first."

The respect between Finucane and Capewell was obvious at the medal ceremony.

For a few days they are rivals before going back to being team-mates.

Finucane described her day as a "rollercoaster". In comparison, Morris' was the mother of all "big dippers".

Powering to the pursuit title was the highlight. You have to remember Morris did not own a road bike until she was almost 20 and had not so much as set foot in a velodrome.

The trained doctor, now 31, has gone on to become a double world individual pursuit champion and is now a Commonwealth gold medallist.

This was the first time the event had been held over 4,000m in the Commonwealth Games, having previously been a 3,000m contest.

There was an individual rivalry between Great Britain team-mates Morris and Knight in the pursuit of glory.

They rode alongside each other in the team squad that won Olympic bronze in Paris in 2024. Morris then defeated Knight in the world final of the 2025 individual pursuit final as she defended her title.

The battle lines had been drawn in the morning session when Knight recorded the fastest qualifying time of 4:25.719, with Morris just outside in 4:25.817.

But Morris produced a commanding performance in the final to clinch gold in a time of 4:24:272.

The medal ceremony was just under an hour later.

Morris had heard her victories played out for GB with a different anthem but she looked to be overcome when celebrating this one with the Welsh national song.

No time to immediately reflect on what she had just achieved though.

There was a quick chance for a picture with the Welsh flag and then off it was to the next task.

The scratch race started just 10 minutes later where Morris lined up with Welsh team-mates Megan Barker and Carys Lloyd.

It looked like they had concocted an almost perfect plan, with Barker going off a few laps out and Morris driving through to finish second behind Australian winner Georgia Baker.

A gold and a silver all in one day. Or so we thought.

Morris had already done some interviews celebrating this fact before she was given the message in the media mixed zone about her demotion.

Morris had been relegated for entering the sprinter's lane when her New Zealand opponent was already there, and Scottish cyclist Erin Boothman was promoted to bronze.

Morris returned to do a couple more interviews, ironically, while the scratch closing ceremony was going on.

Morris reflected on her golden moment.

"It was just a dream," said Morris. "We get that opportunity once every four years, so for it to come together tonight was amazing.

"I have my family and friends in the crowd and the support team from Welsh Cycling were also there.

"I'm going to carry that with me forever, it's amazing."

Morris seemed unaware of her dominance in the race.

"It was only when I crossed the line I knew I'd won the race," said Morris.

"I focused on my ride and tried to execute it well and really leave it all out on the track."

It had been a day of mixed emotions and, when asked to sum up her feelings about the scratch race, Morris was whisked off so we will have to wait for that verdict.

So, disappointment to finish the day but that should not take away from her pursuit domination and golden moment.

Morris is a world champion for a reason and she proved why.

Wales cycling have two special world-class talents in Finucane and Morris.

title: Democratic Socialists of America activists signed pledge to support, defend 'Chinese socialism'
description: People with self-described Democratic Socialists of America ties signed on to support a pro-China statement that extols "Chinese socialism."
fullText:
Multiple self-identified Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-linked individuals signed onto a statement extolling "Chinese socialism."

"We, Friends of Socialist China, aim to support the People's Republic of China and to promote understanding of Chinese socialism," the statement declares, in part.

"The global advance to socialism is indispensable if humanity is to survive and to flourish; humanity needs socialism in order to prevent climate breakdown, end poverty, establish global peace and work towards dismantling structural discrimination and oppression," the statement says, characterizing the "record of the socialist countries" as "overwhelmingly positive."

China, Russia, Iran And North Korea Form 'Axis Of Aggressors' That Could Overwhelm Us, Book Warns

The text asserts that "the continued survival of Chinese socialism is a crucial matter not only for the Chinese people but for all humanity" and declares that "we resolve to support, defend and build understanding of Chinese socialism."

Some of the people listed as signatories include Mirah Wood, who is described as the "Co-Chair Middle East & Africa Subcommittee, DSA International Committee" in the United States, and John McGrath, who is identified as being part of the "DSA International Committee (anti-war)" in the United Kingdom.

Both Wood and McGrath appear on the list as far back as 2022 in archived web pages.

Some of the other names on the list include indication of DSA membership.

Dsa Co-chair Embraces Abolishing Senate, Ice, Borders As Democratic Infighting Escalates

The statement describes the view that socialism leads to oppression as "propaganda" that should be challenged.

It says that "owing largely to the reach and power of capitalist cultural hegemony, socialism is widely considered (particularly in the imperialist heartlands) to be a brutal, authoritarian system that suppresses human creativity and impedes progress. Socialist states — past and present — are portrayed as miserable backwaters, characterized by overzealous secret services, prison camps, thought control, stale uniformity, dictatorship, famines, social conservatism, corruption and poverty. title: Dog walk and expletive text - key findings in Vondrousova anti-doping case
description: The full report into 2023 Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova's four-year ban for refusing a doping test has been released - BBC Sport analyses the key findings.
fullText:
Recent Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova receiving a four-year ban for refusing to take a doping test was a punishment which sent shockwaves through tennis.

The Czech, who became the first unseeded player to win the Wimbledon women's singles title in 2023, would not let a doping control officer into her Prague home to conduct the test in December 2025.

In June, it was announced the 27-year-old would be suspended for four years - the starting point for any player who refuses or evades a test.

On Friday, the independent tribunal which imposed the punishment released its full written report about the case - which it described as a "very unfortunate matter" but which offered "no compelling justification" for a shorter ban.

From how walking her dog undermined her case, to the lack of understanding players seem to have about doping rules, BBC Sport analyses some of the key findings.

Vondrousova, who also reached the French Open final in 2019 and won the Tokyo 2020 Olympics silver medal, claimed she feared for her safety when the doping officer arrived at her flat at 8pm on 3 December.

She was alone in her apartment and told the officer via the intercom that she would not open the door.

The tribunal's report said Vondrousova called her agent to ask about doping protocol, and sent a text message to her boyfriend which said someone from doping control had arrived - using an expletive to describe them.

There is some dispute about what happened next, with the doping officer saying the pair had two exchanges over the intercom, but Vondrousova saying there was only one.

Both sides agree they met face-to-face about 10 minutes later when Vondrousova went outside to walk her Italian Greyhound dog.

That is when Vondrousova reiterated she would not take the test and signed a form which acknowledged her stance.

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) - the body tasked with overseeing a clean and fair sport - said it had little option other than to seek a four-year suspension.

The tribunal agreed with the ITIA. It ruled she had provided "no compelling justification" for refusing a test.

On Friday, the tribunal said: "This is a very unfortunate manner in which the player made a decision in the heat of the moment to refuse doping control, in a state of stress and anxiety, with significant consequences."

Ex-Wimbledon champion Vondrousova given four-year ban

One of the key parts of Vondrousova's mitigation centred around her safety concerns.

The former world number six said she felt scared when the officer approached her door "late at night" without, she claimed, properly identifying themselves or following protocol.

Vondrousova cited the horrific knife attack on her fellow Czech player Petra Kvitova - who was stabbed by an intruder at her home in 2016 - as a reason why she did not open the door.

However, the ITIA contested Vondorousova's case that she felt her safety was at risk, and the reasons why they said they disagreed included:

the area of Prague where she lives is "relatively crime-free"

the comparison with Kvitova's attack was an "exaggeration"

walking her dog was "entirely inconsistent with identifying a potential threat"

The ITIA also noted Vondrousova did not raise any concerns about her safety in the exchanges with her agent and her boyfriend.

In her defence to the tribunal, Vondrousova said another reason why she did not want to open the door was because she suffered from acute stress reaction and an anxiety disorder.

The tribunal acknowledged the situation would have led to anxiety, but said her wider arguments about safety and stress were not "exceptional circumstances".

Vondrousova's case has been another example of how some players have revealed they do not know the doping rules.

After the incident in December, Vondrousova posted an Instagram story in which she accused the officer of not following rules because the call was outside her one-hour whereabouts slot.

The whereabouts rule means players must give a time and location for an hour where they can be tested every day of the year. They are also able to be tested outside this 60-minute slot.

"Unpredictable testing is an essential tool to protect clean sport," ITIA chief executive Karen Moorhouse said in June.

"The tribunal ultimately supported that principle. This case is an important reminder that players can be tested at any time, in any place, and that refusal comes with significant risk."

The tribunal's report noted how Vondrousova said she did not know she could be tested outside the one-hour slot, and claimed she had never been tested at home outside this window before.

She also said her agent did not know out-of-hours testing was possible.

The ITIA argued that "any lack of understanding" of the anti-doping rules by an experienced player like Vondrousova - who has taken 83 tests since 2018 - was "not credible".

Is tennis catching doping cheats or ruining careers?

Vondrousova plans to appeal against the decision and will lodge her case with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) before the 11 August deadline, BBC Sport has been told.

She has not played since January as she dealt with the case, having already dropped to 122nd in the world when her ban was announced in June.

If her appeal is unsuccessful, she will not be able to play again until June 2030.

That means she will be almost 31 years old when free to return - if she wishes.

Whatever happens with the appeal process, Vondrousova's refusal to take the test has already cost her a considerable chunk of what should be the peak years of an impressive career.

It also acts as a serious warning to other players that missing a test will not be tolerated - a deterrent intended by the ITIA, who mission statement is providing 'tennis you can trust'.

title: Colorado small town abandoned after all elected officials resign, water concerns grow
description: Hartman, Colorado, a town of 30 residents, was declared abandoned after all elected officials resigned and its water system became a health hazard.
fullText:
A small town in Colorado has been declared abandoned by the state after its remaining elected officials resigned, leading its troubled water system to become a "health hazard" to its residents, according to state officials.

The Office of the Colorado Secretary of State said the determination was made this week after a public hearing showed that "the Town of Hartman had no Board of Trustees or Town Clerk, was unable to hold a town election, and owned infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents."

"Importantly, not determining that the Town of Hartman is abandoned as contemplated by § 31-3-201(1)(b), C.R.S. (2026), would leave the residents in further legal limbo during a health hazard, with no authority to conduct business, hold elections, or fix their water infrastructure so that clean water can be delivered to the town residents," Deputy Secretary of State Andrew Kline wrote in an abandonment order. "Abandonment is the only legal mechanism in Colorado statute that creates an avenue for residents of the area to receive clean water."

Disneyland Guests Left Scrambling After Water Outage Shuts Bathrooms And Restaurants

Hartman, which has a population of 30 in southeast Colorado, saw its three active trustees resign in January, a day after a brawl erupted between four women following a board of trustees meeting, according to The Denver Post.

"Our safety was more important than having a government," Pam Packer, one of the trustees who resigned, told the newspaper, which also reported that the mayor resigned in October and that Hartman previously was grappling with embezzlement allegations and restraining orders.

Kline said in the abandonment order that in mid-June, "Ms. Jessie Simmons, a self-attested resident, landowner, and elector of the Town of Hartman, submitted a written application to the Secretary of State for determination of abandonment for the Town of Hartman alleging that the town does not have a board of trustees or town clerk, is unable to hold an election, and owns and operates water infrastructure needed to treat and deliver water to residents."

"Ms. Simmons further asserted that as of time of her application, the Town of Hartman had lacked chlorine in its water for over one month and the water was not potable and 'smells horrible.' She stated that the Town of Hartman had been under an order to boil water for months," he wrote.

Experts Reveal How To Avoid Deadly Legionnaires' Disease As Nyc Outbreak Kills 5

At a hearing on July 13, Eric Bergman, the director of the Division of Local Government for the Department of Local Affairs, "testified that he has regional managers throughout the state, and one in Southeast Colorado that has worked extensively with the Town of Hartman for the last 5 or 6 years," according to Kline.

"Mr. Bergman also testified that since 2022, DOLA representatives have been in the Town of Hartman over 30 times helping with elections, turnover, recalls, resignations, budgets, audits, grant administration, and training of new officials. In January of 2026, DOLA received letters of resignation from each of the town's then-Trustees. Since the resignation of these elected officials, no government officials or government remain in the Town of Hartman," the order stated.

"There are no government officials in the Town of Hartman who are authorized to approve contracts, spend funds, appoint replacements, certify elections, or make decisions regarding the Town of Hartman's water system. Mr. Bergman testified there is also no clerk or governing body to call, conduct, or certify a municipal election," it continued.

"According to Mr. Bergman, the Town of Hartman is facing a public health threat. Mr. Bergman testified that the Town of Hartman has been on a boil advisory since last October 2025, and the water currently needs testing and chlorine. The water tank is compromised and needs repair or replacement," Kline also wrote in the order. "There is no one operating the water system at this time. DOLA, along with the Colorado Department of Health and Environment had previously provided grants for more than $1 million to the Town of Hartman to work on the water system. Those funds were reimbursement-based. However, without government officials, the Town is unable to enter any contracts that would enable it to access the grant funds."

The Office of Colorado's Secretary of State said that, following the abandonment order, "All existing streets, avenues, and alleys previously located within the abandoned town that are not owned by a third party shall be vested in the Board of County Commissioners of Prowers County," and that "Ownership of water infrastructure critical for the treatment or delivery of water to residents shall be vested in Prowers County, which shall transfer said infrastructure to an entity whose primary purpose is water treatment or delivery."

title: Fifa scraps controversial World Cup investment plan
description: Football's world governing body abandons plans to sell off stakes in its major competitions after widespread opposition to president Gianni Infantino's proposal.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino says he has scrapped the controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's major competitions, following widespread opposition.

Infantino said it had become clear the project had "created divisions" that are "no longer in the interest" of its original objective.

The Swiss official added: "As a result, this proposal will not proceed."

Infantino had offered all 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.

Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

European football's 55 member associations, Uefa, voted on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.

Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

That came after two other major confederations spoke out against the plans.

Concacaf, which governs football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

Infantino, 56, is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March.

He said he now intends to "bring all interested parties back together" in the "spirit of shared interest" in football.

Despite rejections from Uefa and Concacaf, Fifa initially vowed to continue with its proposals on Friday, saying "nobody is selling football".

However, in announcing the plans had been scrapped, Infantino acknowledged he needed the backing of the majority of Fifa member associations - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour.

That became unlikely when the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf in opposing the plans.

Uefa has 55 votes, Concacaf has 35 and Asia has 46.

If all member associations backed the stance of their governing body, that would have meant 136 nations voting against Infantino's plan.

The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) had said they would discuss Fifa's plan in August.

The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, said it had asked Fifa for "additional information and clarifications" regarding the "scope, structure, governance and possible effects" of the proposals.

Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, with external investors able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

Infantino set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).

A 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan laid out how Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased payout of 24m euros (£20.5m) per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

It mentioned "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".

The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".

There was no mention in the document of the women's game.

Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time on Friday - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.

Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat AFC president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88.

Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.

Prior to this week, it had been anticipated Infantino would be re-elected unopposed. Associations around the world, including some in Europe, had already confirmed their intention to vote for him.

It remains to be seen if the events of this week will result in a mass withdrawal of their support.

In his statement, Infantino reiterated his plan was designed to strengthen members associations, "especially in countries where support is most needed".

He added: "Our purpose has always been - and always will be - to unite and improve."

However, the proposal clearly created division within Fifa itself.

Cordeiro, who represented the world governing body on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup, is the first senior figure at Fifa to resign over the plans.

In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and said he "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value". He added he had no involvement in the proposal.

It is understood Infantino even left some of Fifa's eight vice-presidents in the dark about his plan, which it is claimed could have raised $10bn (£7.5bn).

Lamour called it "the project of one person" and said "a president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them" but this was "the opposite".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account, Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells his critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership.

The Times and Financial Times report Infantino's plan to sell stakes in its competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors.

Uefa publishes its first statement saying football is "not Fifa's to sell", and accuses Fifa of 'crossing a line'.

Fifa issues statement confirming the plans.

Infantino writes to all 211 Fifa member associations saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his plans, but that they must do so by 19 September if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).

Uefa says "Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends."

Uefa's 55 member associations vote to boycott World Cups if Infantino's plan goes ahead.

Concacaf says its 41 member associations also "rejected" the proposal.

Fifa says "nobody is selling football" and vows to continue with the plan.

Asian Football Confederation (AFC) says it "stands in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, though stops short of unequivocally rejecting Infantino's proposal.

A senior adviser to Infantino, Carlos Cordeiro, resigns citing "a bad deal for football" that would "mortgage football's future".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Infantino is the "wrong man" to lead Fifa.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour says the governing body's own administration has been "deceived" about the project.

Infantino releases statement at about 00:30 BST on Saturday, saying the plan will not proceed.

title: Hunter Bell eyes ambitious sweep after 800m gold in Glasgow
description: England's Georgia Hunter Bell eyes an ambitious sweep of gold medals in 2026 after winning the 800m Commonwealth Games title in Glasgow.
fullText:
Georgia Hunter Bell is eyeing an ambitious sweep of gold medals in 2026 after winning the 800m Commonwealth Games title in Glasgow.

England's Hunter Bell dominated the field to add Commonwealth gold to the 1500m world indoor title she won earlier this year in Poland.

The 32-year-old, a training partner of 800m Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, will also race at next month's European Championships and the inaugural Ultimate Championships in September.

"There are four opportunities to win gold this year," Hunter Bell told BBC Sport.

"I am two golds down and two more to go."

Hunter Bell is blossoming later in her career.

Having taken five years out from the sport before returning during the Covid-19 pandemic, she took 1500m bronze at the Paris Olympics before pipping Hodgkinson to silver at last year's World Championships in the 800m.

This, though, is her first outdoor title - in the event Hodgkinson is Olympic champion.

"Every medal is a landmark moment but my first outdoor gold is huge," she said.

Hunter Bell and Kenya's world champion Lilian Odira were the favourites for this title after Hodgkinson opted not to compete. The final was barely a contest with Hunter Bell setting the pace and then kicking on with 200m to go to win by more than a second.

Hodgkinson has instead taken time off before the European Championships in Birmingham, which start on 10 August.

Hunter Bell is only running in the 1500m in that event, denying the chance to see an intriguing race between the pair, but took her opportunity in her friend and training partner's absence.

Though she said the win validates her decision to come to Glasgow, she defended the decision of others to withdraw.

Dina Asher-Smith, Katarina Johnson-Thompson and Matt Hudson-Smith have been other high-profile English absentees.

"Every decision is different per athlete," Hunter Bell said.

"A few weeks ago I had to pull out of London which I was devastated about because I was sick.

"We want to be healthy and racing at all times.

"That is what people don't understand.

"If we could we would be racing non-stop.

"We get incentivised financially, we love it. This is what we train for.

"If we are not showing up there was a reason for that."

Later, Emily Newnham's late surge secured England silver in the 400m hurdles while Jake Minshull also took silver in the men’s race.

title: Same start but different outlook at Rangers as McInnes era begins
description: Derek McInnes insists Rangers will improve after his team's Scottish Premiership draw at Dundee United.
fullText:
A year ago, Russell Martin tore strips off his Rangers team after an opening day draw at Motherwell.

Two managers and plenty of disappointment later, it was the same result but a different tone at Dundee United as the Derek McInnes era started in underwhelming fashion.

The former Aberdeen, Kilmarnock and Hearts boss stressed the need for time and for further additions as he guides the Ibrox outfit through a summer of transition.

"It's one game," he told Sky Sports following a 1-1 draw on Friday. "I'm not really interested in what's happened previously, but from my point of view, we are going to get better as we go along."

Having gone behind to Lachlan Rose's first-half effort, Rangers improved after the break and equalised through Thelo Aasgaard, but failed to capitalise and were fortunate not to concede late on when Jesse Randall dinked a tame effort straight at debutant goalkeeper Ivor Pandur.

"It's disappointing - we've dropped a couple of points, but we weren't good enough to get all three," McInnes added.

"We've got to have more trust in what we're doing, keep our shoulder to the wheel and do simple things better."

Dundee Utd hold Rangers in Premiership opener

Will Scottish Premiership return to two-team title tussle?

Scottish Premiership is back - here's why you shouldn't miss it

Sportsound : A share of the spoils at Tannadice as the Premiership returns

Former Rangers striker Steven Thompson agreed with McInnes that there is no need to panic.

"It's not the result Rangers wanted, but it is a point away from home at a difficult venue," he said on BBC Radio Scotland. "Other teams will come here and find it very difficult.

"At this point in the season, there's no knee-jerk [reaction] or anything here.

"It's not what McInnes wants, but it's the first game of the season. There will be time to judge once he gets the players he wants and once he gets more work done on the training ground.

"He will have learned a lot from his players tonight."

On a night where Pandur, centre-back Ben Godfrey and former Hearts duo Cammy Devlin and Lawrence Shankland all made their debuts from the start, it was a glimpse into what this new-look Rangers side might look like under McInnes.

Summer signings Dan Neil and Ross McCrorie also came on as substitutes and McInnes made it clear there will be further additions in the weeks to come.

However, former Rangers man Andy Halliday saw what he believes to have been flaws in McInnes' tactical set-up.

"No matter how many defenders you play with, the main fundamental is being compact, and I thought Rangers were the furthest thing from compact," he said on Sportsound.

"All the best individuals, other than Thelo Aasgaard, were Dundee United players.

"Rangers are a work in progress, I think they'll still make additions to try and improve, but it certainly wasn't the start they were looking for."

With Godfrey going off with a hamstring complaint and uncertainty over whether new signing Olwethu Makhanya will receive a visa for Thursday's trip to Jagiellonia Bialystok in Europa League qualifying, Rangers are after defensive recruits, but it is in wide areas that McInnes is most keen to strengthen.

Djeidi Gassama started on the left at Tannadice but was hooked at half-time, and Rangers finished with Mohamed Diomande and Aasgaard playing narrow.

"I thought second half as the game got stretched, we had opportunities to play in the spaces and we need people with the ability to go past [defenders]," McInnes told Sky.

"We still would like a winger to go get at people, make a difference and get people on the back foot.

"We never quite had that and we're working hard to bring those types of players to the club. Our strikers are all dependant on service. We're working hard and we know what we want."

South Korea's Haeran Ryu birdied the 18th to bounce back from a poor start and end the second round as leader of the AIG Women's Open at Royal Lytham & St Annes.

The 25-year-old, aiming to become only the fifth woman in history to claim three majors in a calendar year, is one shot clear of Japan's Shiho Kuwaki.

Earlier this month, Ryu claimed her second major in the space of two weeks at the Evian Championship, and her remarkable major form has continued at the Open.

Despite being three over for the day through five holes, she sank five birdies to shoot two under par and build on her opening-round score of 66.

"The last hole is so important as it is always good for tomorrow, I always want to make a good score on the last hole," Ryu told BBC Sport.

"I've had two birdies on it, which is a good thing.

"I just stayed patient after that [the tough start] and I made some birdies to finish under par. I am so happy now."

Women's Open third round tee-times

Kuwaki, who finished Thursday two shots behind leader Jeeno Thitikul, carded a one-under-par round to take advantage of Thitikul's dropped shots.

Following a spectacular seven-under-par 64, Thailand's Thitikul shot a two-over-par 73.

American Yealimi Noh joins world number two Thitikul on five under par after shooting 70.

England's Lottie Woad is in a strong position to compete for a first major title despite a disappointing end to her second round.

The 22-year-old, who arrived as one of the favourites, ended the day on two under par.

Woad's bogey-free opening round of 69 was followed up by a score of 71, which included three birdies on the front nine.

However, two dropped shots on the back nine - one on 17 - leaves her five shots back.

England's Charley Hull went round in even par to remain on two under par, while world number one Nelly Korda shot 68 to recover from an opening-round two-over-par 73.

Three-time major champion Lydia Ko is also well placed to make a move from one under par, as is England's Mimi Rhodes, who recovered from two early bogeys to sink three birdies.

Who are the best active players never to have won a major in the women's game?

For many, Hull and Thitikul would be the first names that come to mind.

Hull has finished runner-up in five majors, with her most recent near-miss coming in June's US Open.

Her solid opening round at the Open left her two under par and in a strong position to challenge for a maiden major title.

A tricky back nine on her second round ended in style, as a birdie from the bunker on the 17th was followed by a par at the last.

It was not a round that ever truly caught fire, despite featuring three birdies, but it keeps Hull firmly in contention.

"I am really looking forward to it [the weekend], it's going to be loads of fun," Hull said.

"I feel like now my nerves have settled down. My back was actually playing up for me a little bit, a little bit sore, that's why I think I wasn't getting through the ball how I wanted to."

Former world number one Thitikul, who has 11 top-10 finishes in majors, said the stronger wind compared with Thursday played a part in her scoring.

She lipped out for birdie on the sixth and seventh before a lengthy par save on the 15th prevented back-to-back bogeys.

Her faultless opening round contained no dropped shots, but that run ended on the third hole of her second round.

Thitikul's only birdie of the day came on 12, but there could have been more. She also lipped out with her final putt, which would have pulled another shot back.

Having spoken previously about struggling to cope with the noise of finally winning a major, Thitikul may be content for the spotlight to shift elsewhere after her stunning opening round.

Hull responds to criticism of prank on caddie

Following an opening two-over-par 73, Korda needed to hit the ground running in her second round to get back into contention.

Korda's victory at the US Women's Open in June gave her a chance to complete the career Grand Slam, achieved by winning all five women's major titles.

A run of four birdies in six holes began with a putt from about 20 feet on the fourth.

Another lengthy putt from the edge of the green on the 11th continued what was becoming a sensational round.

"That's 36 [holes] in, 36 holes to go. You never know what's going to happen. It's golf. It's links golf," Korda said.

"I am just going to try to have the same attitude I had today going into the weekend."

Having won the first two majors of the year, Korda is also in contention to become only the fifth woman in history to claim three majors in a calendar year.

That looked unlikely after Thursday, but her performance on Friday showed why she is a four-time major champion with the chance to achieve something special.

Her round still contained three bogeys and her last birdie came on 13, preventing a further climb up the leaderboard.
